questions.enonce_markdown:
Distinguish between each of the following:

(i) Red blood cells and white blood cells

(ii) Arteries and veins. *(5, 6 marks)*
questions.corrige_markdown:
**(i) Red blood cells and white blood cells**

| Red blood cells (erythrocytes) | White blood cells (leucocytes) |
|---|---|
| Biconcave disc shape, fixed shape | Irregular shape (can change shape) |
| **No nucleus** (in mammals) | **Have a nucleus** (lobed or rounded) |
| Contain **haemoglobin**, so appear red | Contain no haemoglobin; colourless |
| Very numerous (about 5 million per $\mathrm{mm^3}$) | Much fewer (about 5 000 - 10 000 per $\mathrm{mm^3}$) |
| Smaller (about 7 $\mu$m) | Larger, of different sizes |
| Transport oxygen (and some carbon dioxide) | Defend the body: phagocytosis and production of antibodies |
| Made in the red bone marrow; live about 120 days | Made in the bone marrow and lymph nodes; live from hours to months |

**(ii) Arteries and veins**

| Arteries | Veins |
|---|---|
| Carry blood **away from the heart** | Carry blood **towards the heart** |
| Carry **oxygenated** blood (except the pulmonary artery) | Carry **deoxygenated** blood (except the pulmonary vein) |
| **Thick, muscular and elastic walls** | **Thin walls** with little muscle |
| **Narrow lumen** | **Wide lumen** |
| **No valves** (except at the base of the aorta and pulmonary artery) | **Valves present** to prevent backflow |
| Blood flows under **high pressure** in pulses | Blood flows under **low pressure**, smoothly |
| Deep in the body | Many lie near the surface |

questions.enonce_markdown: Explain how the structure of the red blood cell is adapted to its function of transport of respiratory gases. *(5 marks)*
questions.corrige_markdown:
The red blood cell transports **oxygen** (as oxyhaemoglobin) from the lungs to the tissues, and some carbon dioxide from the tissues to the lungs. It is adapted as follows:

1. It is **biconcave in shape**, which gives a **large surface area to volume ratio** for rapid diffusion of gases.
2. It **contains haemoglobin**, a pigment that **combines loosely and reversibly with oxygen** to form oxyhaemoglobin in the lungs and releases it in the tissues.
3. It has **no nucleus (and few organelles)** in mammals, which leaves **more room for haemoglobin** and so carries more oxygen.
4. It is **small and flexible**, so it can **squeeze through narrow capillaries** and bring oxygen close to the cells.
5. It has a **thin cell membrane**, so gases diffuse in and out easily, and it is very **numerous**, increasing the oxygen carried.

questions.enonce_markdown: Why are people of blood group O and blood group AB regarded as universal donors and universal recipients respectively? *(4 marks)*
questions.corrige_markdown:
The ABO groups depend on **antigens on the red blood cells** (A and B) and **antibodies in the plasma** (anti-A and anti-B).

* **Group O** red blood cells have **no A or B antigens**. When they are given to a person of any group, there is **nothing for the recipient's antibodies to attack**, so no agglutination (clumping) occurs. Group O is therefore the **universal donor**.
* **Group AB** blood has **both A and B antigens** on the red cells but **neither anti-A nor anti-B antibodies in the plasma**. A person of group AB therefore has **no antibodies to agglutinate** donor red cells of group A, B, AB or O, so can receive blood from any group. Group AB is therefore the **universal recipient**.
